video_title: Gary Gallagher: American Civil War, Slavery, Lincoln, Grant & Lee | Lex Fridman Podcast #499
transcript: - You cannot control what a great military event can set loose. More battle casualties than US forces had suffered in every war combined down to that point happened in two days. Two and a half months after that, George B. McClellan's army engaged with Lee's army in what came to be called the Seven Days Battles at Richmond, 36,000 casualties. So those two together just showed that this was gonna be on a totally different scale. He added a psychological twist. What, what Grant envisioned his doing, and Sheridan actually did it in the Shenandoah Valley before Sherman did it in Georgia, is go into an agriculturally productive area, burn the mills, kill the livestock, destroy the crops, lay waste to it so that it can't be a logistical support of the Confederacy anymore. Sheridan did it in the Shenandoah Valley, and then Sherman did it in Georgia. But Sherman said, "But I'm also going to break them psychologically. I'm gonna show them that my army can go wherever it wants to go whenever it wants to go, and there's nothing Jefferson Davis can do about it." The great forces are all that matters and individuals don't really matter notion of history I think is ridiculous. Individuals really matter. For the United States, Lincoln and Grant matter beyond calculation- ... in this war. And on the Confederate side, if you take Lee out of the picture, the war doesn't last nearly as long as it does. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. - The following is a conversation with Gary Gallagher, a historian of the American Civil War. This is the Lex Fridman Podcast. To support it, please check out our sponsors in the description where you can also find links to contact me, ask questions, give feedback, and so on. And now, dear friends, here's Gary Gallagher. The American Civil War broke out in 1861. What were the causes of the Civil War? Could it have been avoided, or was it inevitable? - I don't know if anything is inevitable in history, but it's certainly safe to say that the conditions were in place to make it possible- ... by the winter of 1860, '61, and the conditions that made it possible were all related to the institution of slavery and its effects both in the states where slavery was allowed and the states where it was not allowed. And there had been a series of tensions that grew in the decade preceding the 1850s. It's not that one side wants to get rid of slavery and the other side wants to protect slavery. I'm talking about the white people in the United States now who would be making the political decisions. It's a question of whether slavery was going to be able to expand into federal territories. That is what really created the starkest difference between the two sections in the 1850s, even in the late 1840s. The issues that came to most, uh, perilous a point in the view of many people then had to do with whether slavery would be allowed only where it already existed, or would it be allowed to expand. If it could expand, then it seemed that it might be conceivable at some point even that the slaveholding states could end up with a majority. They were in a minority by 1860, '61 and feeling beleaguered, feeling threatened. They'd long since lost the population race to the free states. Early in the nation, the most powerful states were slaveholding states. Virginia was by far the most important state. Four of the first five presidents were from Virginia, all slaveholders, all prominent members of the slaveholding class. Those days were long gone by the late 1850s. - So that's an important thing to say. It wasn't before the Civil War a discussion about abolishing slavery. It's about whether slavery, the institution of slavery should be expanded. - Allowed to expand into federal territories. There, there is a portion of the white population that is adamantly in favor of getting rid of slavery immediately. The abolitionists, they... There was even a political party called the Liberty Party, that ran a candidate in 1840 and they got a handful of thousand votes. They reached their high point in 1844. They got about two and a half percent of the vote. The abolitionists are a tiny minority among the— even in the North, tiny minority among the white people of the United States. The African American population, nearly four million of them by 1860, of course, would have embraced it instantly and yearned for it. But in the white population, the abolitionists are a tiny minority. They are much despised even across much of the North because they were seen as agitators who roiled the Union and deepened rifts that might bring a significant political break. - So how did this escalate to a civil war, this almost policy discussion about the institution of slavery? How did it actually escalate? - It escalated into a civil war because in the presidential election of 1860... There'd been two party systems in the United States. The first party system, the Republicans, the Jeffersonian Republicans versus the Federalists. After that, there was, the two parties were the Whig Party against the Democratic Party. The Democratic Party grew out of the Jeffersonian Republican Party. It's the same party. The Whig Party foundered to a significant degree on the issue of slavery. How do you maintain a national party that has a wing in the Southern states and has a wing in the Northern free states that can handle the issue of slavery? The Democrats managed to do that. The Whigs could not do it, and so the Whig Party ran their last candidate in 1852, presidential candidate, significant candidate. And the Republican Party emerged in the mid-1850s, took most of the old Whigs into the Republican ranks and one of the Republican, the key Republican platform plank was no expansion of slavery into the territories. Not abolish slavery, no expansion. That was the key in 1856 when they ran their first candidate. In 1860, that is again the key plank in the Republican platform. The Republican platform in 1860 says where slavery exists it will continue, but it cannot expand into the territories. When white Southerners saw that, that meant that they were doomed to become an increasingly minority section in the nation, and you would have a federal government increasingly dominated by the free states that could then do the one thing that the white South could not countenance, and that is tamper with the institution of slavery in the South. The presidential election of 1860 brought the destruction of the last national party, which was the Democrats. They couldn't even settle on a candidate, so you end up with a Northern Democratic candidate running, Stephen A. Douglas, and a Southern candidate running. The convention fractured and John C. Breckinridge ran on the, on the Southern Democrat platform. You had a Unionist candidate running who just didn't wanna talk about slavery, let's talk about the Union, and you had Lincoln running as a Republican. When Lincoln won, the white South looked at Lincoln winning. Here's a guy who has said that he doesn't think slavery would expand, but he'd said more than that. He scared the white South more because in 1858, both Lincoln and William Henry Seward, these are two prominent, prominent Republicans, had said basically in separate speeches, the House Divided Speech on Lincoln's part, the Irrepressible Conflict Speech on Seward's part, that the nation could not continue in the long term half slave and half free. And everybody in the South knew which way they wanted it to be. They would want it to be no slavery. And so Lincoln's election scared the white South enough so that seven of the 15 slave-holding states seceded in response to Lincoln's election. They seceded between December 20th, when South Carolina went out, and the end of February. You had the deep South went out. - What was the general view amongst the populace towards slavery? Let's kind of lay it out. Let's you know, for the audience looking back, let's put ourselves in the mind space of how people saw the world, how people saw slavery, how people saw African Americans. - Well, the baseline among the white Americans, there were about 31, shade more than 31 million Americans in 1860 for the census of 1860. About four million of them were African Americans, three and a half million of those enslaved in the South. Anyway, among the white population, the average attitude toward Black people is what we would call profoundly prejudiced. Doesn't matter whether you... A lot of people think this is a Southern white thing. They're the only ones who were prejudiced. By our standards, the overwhelming majority of people in the free states were also deeply prejudiced. It's important to keep in mind that attitudes towards slavery and attitudes toward race do not, they're not necessarily the same. I mean, you could be against slavery and still be prejudiced against Black people. By our standards, many abolitionists were prejudiced against Black people. They... But the overwhelming majority of the white North, in the North, often had a hard time getting my students to understand the demographics in 1860. The free states in 1860 were more than 98% white. 98% white. African Americans are a tiny minority in the free states. Black people lived in the 15 slaveholding states in 1860. Most of the white North, by our standards, was very prejudiced. They were against the expansion of slavery into the territories because they thought that would circumscribe white opportunities to make an economic life in these federal territories, and they didn't want that to happen. About 45% of the people who lived in the free states were Democrats. Most Democrats had no problem with slavery. I mean, absolutely no problem with the institution of slavery. There would be more problems among Republicans, especially with extension of slavery, although many Democrats, white Democrats in the North were against that as well. The white South was overwhelmingly in favor of slavery. You often read the argument, the kind of neo-Confederate argument that they'll talk about how most Confederate soldiers didn't own slaves. That's true. The a large majority of families in the South did not own a single slave. But all white Southerners had a stake in slavery. They had a stake in it as a form of labor control, but more important than that, they had a stake in it as a means of social control. They knew, no matter what they said later in the Jim Crow era of how happy Black people were in the institution of slavery, they knew that Black people, of course, did not want to be enslaved, and they were afraid of what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore. They had in the backs of their minds Haiti. Is that what's gonna... If you live in one of the coastal districts of South Carolina where 90% of the residents are enslaved and you're a white person, you probably don't sleep all that soundly at night if you think there's any chance that the Black people are not gonna remain under the control of the white people. So all white people in the South had a stake in slavery, not just some. All of them did, and there were all kinds of ways that it would go back and forth. If you were a modest farmer and grew a little bit of cotton, you didn't have your own cotton gin, you... but your more wealthy neighbor had a gin, could gin your cotton there, and then you would take your turn on the slave patrol, the slave patrols. So there's a reciprocity in that regard. - This is perhaps a bit outside the scope of what we'll talk about today, but just to lay out the context on slavery in general in human history, we should say that slavery was ubiquitous. It existed in virtually every major civilization in the history of humans. Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, the Islamic world, Africa, the Americas, North and South America. We should also say something that, as I was looking into this, another big topic, which is the Atlantic slave trade. And it was surprising to me, the stat I wasn't aware of, I would venture to say most Americans probably don't know, that only 4% of African slaves were brought to North America, to the United States. - Brazil is the main destination. - Brazil, the Caribbean was over 90%, 4.9 million in Brazil, 4 million in the Caribbean, and it was also the last of the Americas to abolish the slave trade. So only 4% of the Atlantic slave trade went to the United States. So there's-- the story of human slavery is one that reaches deep into our history and geographically is much larger than we often study in the context of the United States. - One thing the war, the Civil War, which I'll just call the war for the rest of our discussion, I mean, one thing it did was end slavery in four years in the United States. Whereas in the absence of that war, it might have gone on for decades. I think the United States would have had the ignominious distinction of being the last place to get rid of slavery, would have been after Brazil, would have been after Spanish Cuba, because it was thriving in the United States in 1860. It was making the transition from cash crop agriculture- ... to other, to industrial applications and other applications growing of non-- not growing, growing just cotton and rice and sugar. It was-- There was a time in the literature when people argued that the war was needless, the Civil War was needless because slavery was on its way out. That's absolutely wrong. It was not on its way out. It was thriving. Lincoln said at one point he thought it might have lasted another fifty years, and I don't know how many years it would have lasted, but I think it would have lasted longer than it did in either Cuba or Brazil if it hadn't, if the war hadn't taken place. - So slavery was flourishing in the United States from- - Flourishing. - ... from an economics perspective- ... especially. - The wealthiest part... The 1860 census is our friend, and it tells us that the people who controlled the most wealth in the United States were slaveholders, and their property in slaves alone, not their other holdings, not their land holdings, just property in slaves were valued at about three billion dollars. The value of all industries, all railroads, all of that put together, fewer than two point five billion dollars. So the people who controlled the most wealth, by far, were the slaveholding class. - So it was the most valuable industry in the United States, and perhaps it is the reason, Again, a bit out of scope, but maybe it helps lay out the land. Let's look at the nineteenth century. So most slave-owning societies of the era were able to abolish slavery without people dying at the mass scale that we'll discuss. So Britain freed eight hundred thousand slaves in 1833- ... By buying their freedom. Russia freed twenty-three million serfs in 1861 with a decree, so legally. Brazil, which imported more than ten times as many enslaved Africans as the United States, abolished slavery in 1888 through basic ordinary legislation. No violence. Why did the US have a civil war with an estimated seven hundred and fifty thousand people dead in order to abolish slavery? - Yes. That's-- Let's talk just for a second about the seven hundred and fifty thousand dead soldiers we're talking about. The number for years was six hundred and eighteen thousand, and that's been revised lately. I think we're probably certainly more than seven hundred thousand. By far the bloodiest war in, in our history as a percentage of the population off the charts, by far the bloodiest. I think there's a big difference between Great Britain doing it and the United States doing it, is Great Britain did it in other places. There weren't millions of enslaved people in Great Britain at the time. It's-- I think, for them, it might have been a little bit easier to free enslaved people who don't live among you than it... In the United States, the ante is up for the Confederacy because they, the enslaved people lived here, and I think they were, a lot of them were afraid of them and what would happen if they weren't enslaved anymore. The war goes from... It doesn't begin as a war to end slavery. There's a major shift in the war, begins in the summer of 1862, where you add to the war. The war aim for the United States initially is to suppress the rebellion, which is what they called this. They didn't call it the Civil War for the most part during the war. It's the War of the Rebellion. That's the goal initially. As the war goes on and becomes costlier and more all-encompassing, they decide that they're not gonna be able to suppress the rebellion unless they also strike at slavery, because slavery underpins the Confederate war-making capacity. You have enslaved labor that keeps the economy going and allows the Confederacy to mobilize between eighty-five and ninety percent of all their white military-aged males. It's an astonishing mobilization. It's only possible because enslaved labor keeps the economy going. If you take that enslaved labor away, it deals a significant blow to the Confederate economy and, and by extension, to its ability to wage a nineteenth century war. - So the Emancipation Proclamation was in part a military strategy. - Abraham Lincoln based it entirely on his war-making power as commander-in-chief in a time of open rebellion. His inclination, there's no-- He's often been criticized for not including the soaring language he was capable of in the Emancipation Proclamation. One historian likened it to a bill of lading. It had all the soaring language of a bill of lading. He did that on purpose. He did it because he, he doesn't have the power to strike at slavery in the absence of a war. The president doesn't. And he did it because he knows that he can't win the war with only Republicans in the army. He needs to keep Democrats on board with the war as well. They're not in favor of emancipation. The one way that they might accept it is as a tool to help achieve union, and to do that we've got to strike at the rebels this way, strike at slavery. That will hurt their war effort, and it will also punish the people who brought on the war, and that would make... So Lincoln hoped that by basing it strictly on his war power, it might be more widely accepted across all parts of the loyal states and not as controversial as it was. It was still intensely controversial. It alienated many Democrats when he issued it, who said, "You're changing what this war is about. We're willing to shed our blood and maybe risk our lives to restore the union of the founders. I'm not gonna risk my life to free a Black person." That's a very, very common attitude among Democrats. - So what did the Emancipation Proclamation actually do? It emphasized the freeing of slaves in the South. - It's even more complicated than that. The only place that Lincoln said he had the power as the war leader to strike at slavery is where the rebels were actually still in rebellion and in control. So any place where the US Army was in control, any place-- He said that it is in essence United States territory now. I can't free them there because I don't have the power. I can only free them where we don't have the power. So he exempted parts of states and areas in the South that it didn't apply to as of the moment he signed it. Going forward, any place that the United States Army went where it hadn't been on January 1st, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation applied and enslaved people would be freed by it. At the, literally at the time he signed it, he didn't free anybody because he's only saying, "I can free them where we're not in control. We have to be in control for this to have effect and for this to have power." - So in part, this is why the army was the boundary which the freeing was happening. - It's, it's, it's absolutely the boundary, and Congress had already passed what was called the Second Confiscation Act. It passed this in July of 1862 that announced that all enslaved people belonging to rebels were free. It didn't apply to people who could prove they were unionists living in the South and owned slaves. Lincoln didn't make that distinction in the Emancipation Proclamation. His proclamation is broader than the Second Confiscation Act was. - Okay. There's so many tangents we can take, but let's zoom out once again. There's a difference between cause, as you've talked about, cause and motivation. - Absolutely. - Quite a large number of people volunteered to fight. - In fact, a majority of all the soldiers who fought on both sides were volunteers during the Civil War. About 3 million served, 2.2 million in the United States, 800, 900,000 in the Confederacy. It's, again, I talk about things that are hard to get students to understand. This is one of them. They have to separate... The causation and motivation are often conflated, and not just by students but also by lots of talking heads on newscasts in the United States who don't know anything about United States history- ... but know what they know. In terms of causation, if you take slavery out of the picture, there is no Civil War, period. That's not a long conversation you need. You ask the question. That's the answer. Let's go to the next question. The next question is, okay, so were most white people motivated to put on blue uniforms because they wanted to kill slavery? The answer to that is no, they were not. They were motivated to put on blue uniforms to salvage the Union, which they saw as a unique gift that the founding generation, based on the bloodshed in the American Revolution, had bequeathed the successive generations. And the two key parts of what the Union meant for them was, number one, you had a voice in your own government, and someone will always say now to me, "Well, but women couldn't vote." That's right. The people who could vote by our standards were limited in the 19th century, but within the context of the Western world in 1860, the United States had by far the broadest franchise, by far. And so they argued that's one thing the Union gives us, and it also gives us the chance to rise economically. Doesn't guarantee that you can succeed, but it means you're not doomed to be what your father was. And those are worth fighting for. And so I will put on a uniform so the slave-holding aristocrats and oligarchs, which is what they called them, of the South, they said they're not... They don't really believe in democracy. It's an oligarchy- ... in the South. It's a slavery-based oligarchy, and we know which way Europe's going, they said. The revolutions of the 1840s failed in Europe. Europe's going the wrong way. They're going toward more aristocracy, more oligarchy, more... And we are the last hope. When Lincoln spoke of the last best hope of Earth, which he did in one of his most memorable phrases, he's meaning that the United States is a beacon of small D democracy in a Western world that seems to be turning the other way. And those soldiers, it meant, it meant it was that important to them. They are citizens in a republic that people shed blood to establish, and we can't let it go. Part of the compact is I'm a citizen. I derive these benefits from this republic, from the Union. I can have a voice in government. I can rise economically or have the chance to. I owe my service to that republic. That's what most of them would've said if you'd pressed them on why they're doing it. Doesn't mean everybody was on fire with ideology that way. Some guys would say, "Well, you know what? I'm broke, and I'm gonna get fed and clothed in the army." But this sense of exceptionalism, exceptionalism's unpopular now in the United States, but Americans had a sense of themselves as a truly exceptionalist society within the context of the Western world. - And as a small aside terminology-wise, blue is the Union or what we think of as the United States, and red is the Confederacy. - Yes. On the maps, the Confederate units are red blocks. And the United States units are blue blocks. That's right. - And, uh - That is correct. - And the North and the South is another way we'll refer to it just to clarify. - And let me have a very brief rant on North and South. I prefer to see this as a war between two mid-19th-century republics, One of which didn't last very long and spent its whole life in the midst of a great war. There were 15 slaveholding states in 1860. Only 11 of them seceded from the United States. - Even though there's 13 stars. We'll talk about that. - We'll talk about that demented notion of things in just a minute, but only 11 leave. So there are four slaveholding states in the United States: Kentucky, and Missouri, and Maryland, and Delaware remain in the United States. So it's not just North versus South. Those states are all part of the South. It's the United States versus the Confederacy. - But see how you referred to it as the United States. So the Union is also referred to as the United States - That's correct. Yes, yes - But the Confederacy was, as you write about, a set of people who also had a sense of nationalism, pride - Well, and took their founding document. I mean, it took the whole summer of 1787 in Philadelphia, that hot, steamy, humid summer of 1787 to come up with the Constitution. The Confederates did it quickly 'cause they basically had the US Constitution here, a blank piece of paper over here ... copied most of the Constitution over here, just changed the parts that they needed to make sure slavery was protected, and you didn't have the wrong kind of tariffs and so forth. That's one reason they could do it so quickly. It's absolutely based on the government they've been thriving under, which is under the United States Constitution. Both sides claimed they were the true inheritors of the revolutionary generation. That was one of their... They all... Jefferson Davis loved the Declaration of Independence. The Declaration is Abraham Lincoln's favorite document. They just liked different parts of it - So we should think of this as two republics - I argue that. That makes many people very angry - I will make many people angry today - They say that I am conferring legitimacy on the Confederacy that they don't deserve, and my response to that is they have a national government. They have a Senate. They have a Congress. They have an army. They have a navy. They have departments. They... It's... It walks like a duck. It quacks like a duck. In the end, it's a slaughtered duck faster than it would've been because the United States military forces crushed it - We should say that you are respected, admired, loved by most people on both sides in, from a perspective sense. You're deeply respected by historians of Civil War and just historians of American history. But of course, when you do your job well on a controversial topic in a controversial period of human history- ... you're going to get, hopefully an equal amount of critics on both sides. And that's when you do your job well. So sometimes when we speak today, some of the controversial, quote-unquote, controversial things that you express are controversial from that small minority of folks on both sides for different reasons - Yes. I won't be... One of my favorite pieces of hate mail I got was an email where this guy, I had... He was upset that I referred to the Confederacy as a slave-holding republic that was... And he said that he hoped I would develop virulent pancreatic cancer and die a horrible death. Not just regular pancreatic cancer. He wanted virulent pancreatic cancer And then he signed his name and said he'd be happy to talk to me anytime I wanted to - Yeah. I'm sure that would be a wonderful conversation But there's also really strong senses throughout, throughout the United States, the United States, of the, this diversity of opinion of what is the United States - Of course. Yes - And that's where the passion is really rooted - Both sides claim... In the election of 1860, Douglas talked about how much he loved the Union. Lincoln talked about how much he loved the Union. Breckinridge talked about how much he loved the Union. They're all... And John Bell, who's the Unionist, the Constitutional Union- That's all he talked about. They just had different versions of what the Union was - And that's why I love this country. I think it's the greatest country on Earth, and it has a bunch of people that very strongly disagree with each other. Of course, hopefully never again escalating to the degree that it did during this period of time. So we talked about the blue people on the map and the red people on the map. It may be a silly thing to ask, but sticking with the motivation, why would, let's say, a farm boy in Ohio- ... want to die for the Union? - That is the most important, and I didn't even ask you to ask that question. That's the, that's the hardest thing- - Let's be honest. You paid me a lot of money to ask that question, yeah. - I didn't think it was so much. - Okay. I'm sorry. Go ahead. I won't distract. - No. The, I tell my students at the beginning of my Civil War class that if they couldn't explain, I didn't use Ohio. I said, "If you can't explain why a farmer from Vermont- ... would put on a blue uniform and pick up a musket to make South Carolina come back in, why didn't he just say, 'Great. South Carolina's gone. I never liked them anyway. This is a better union.' If you can't explain that, then you can't understand the Civil War." And the key to that, I'll come back to it, is union because he would've said, "If we allow South Carolina to go That means that other places could go and you could dismantle. And the only reason they're going is because they didn't like who was elected president. They didn't say that Lincoln was corrupt. They didn't say Republicans bought the election. They just didn't like who won the election. And so if the republic is so fragile that it can't have an election without having the people who didn't like who won leave, then the founders had wasted their time, the revolution was for nothing, all that bloodshed meant nothing. You had to step up and save this precious republic that had put in place by the revolutionary generation and gave its citizens the benefits that I've already talked about. That's why they would put on a uniform and risk their life, because they believed a citizen... These are citizen soldiers. We don't know what that means so much now. because we have a professional military establishment now. Not-- I mean, even when I was younger, there was still a draft, and but that's gone now. And so we don't understand what the concept of citizen soldier was, that you owe something back to the republic that has conveyed these things to you, and that's why the guy from Vermont or New Hampshire or Ohio would put on a uniform and go into military service. - Is it possible for us to understand that level of love of nation and believe in nation? Is this, is this very distant from what America is today? - I actually think many people probably still feel that way, but they're not the ones who are on television- ... most of the time. Republicans in the midst of the war commented about the fact that even with this gigantic conflict going on, immigration continued at a high level. People coming into a nation that was in the middle of a great war. And they said, "This is a testament to the promise of the United States." And I think that promise continues. I mean, we've argued about... As with so many things, Americans have no sense of history. They believe we've never argued about immigration before. We've always argued about immigration, with some people always saying, "Shut the door. They're ruining us. The Italians are ruining us. The Irish are Catholics. They're ruining us. God, the Southern Europeans are even worse than, than the Irish were." It's-- The people change, the arguments stay very much the same, and I think it's really telling that in the midst of the war, people would say, "Look at our republic. It is-- It offers so much to people that even in the midst of this great war, they're still coming- ... to the United States." - And like you said, both sides, both these republics claimed, for example, George Washington. - Yes. They both claim... I'll leave it at that. They both claim George Washington. They wanted to be right with the man, which is what George Washington was. He's the indispensable man, no question. Both sides wanted him on their side. They both quoted Thomas Jefferson, although Confederates were a little more leery of Jefferson 'cause he's too complicated for them sometimes. But no, they wanted to be right with the founders and claimed to be right with the founders. The Confederates would say, "The Constitution allowed slavery. What are you talking about we're out of step with the Constitution? We're in step with the Con- You're the ones who are out of step with the Constitution." - What about the topic of states' rights? At the very least- - I love state rights. State rights... I mean, I love the way people use it with the Civil War. They associate it solely with Southern states- ... of course. State rights is always available in United States history for somebody who's not happy with what the federal government is doing. During the War of 1812, it was New England that most often talked- ... about resorting to state rights. They had a convention where they sort of wandered over towards secession territory in the Hartford Convention. We think of it as state rights because as you lead up to the Civil War, you hear con- white Southerners talking about it all the time. "We need our state rights." I always love to ask people who say that, "What are all the state rights? Give me-- List the state rights that the white South is concerned." You know, "Give me the top three. No, really, just give me the top two." There's only one. The state right that they're worried about is the right of their state to interpose its power between a federal government that might try to interfere with slavery and a state government that wants to maintain it. That's the state right that matters then. Northern states also resorted to state rights during this, the ramp-up to the Civil War, with what were called personal liberty laws. They tried to interpose their state power in between a federal government that would use its power to to force escaped, enslaved people back into slavery. It's whoever's unhappy with the federal government, the concept of state rights is available, and both sides used it. - And of course, the beautiful, dark, ironic hypocrisy was illustrated by the Confederacy when they were the first to pass a national draft in American history. - Like, irony is wonderful- ... in history. Another thing that I love to teach is that the most intrusive central government in American history, by far, until deep into the 20th century, was the Confederate central government, because it had to do things to keep the war going that it couldn't have done unless the central government stepped in, such as passing the first national conscription law in American history.
